Chatter

A multi-tenant SaaS chat platform, embeddable widget, agent web panel, and GraphQL/REST API, designed to give Nepali businesses Intercom-class customer engagement without the global price tag.

Overview

Chatter is a B2B SaaS customer-engagement platform. Businesses install an embeddable widget on their site with a JS snippet; their agents log into a web panel to triage conversations, manage contacts, run email/SMS campaigns, and track tasks. The product is multi-tenant, one panel manages unlimited apps for different sites, and sits on a GraphQL and REST API surface, with end-to-end encrypted message payloads (JWE).

At a glance
  • Role: UX/UI designer, sole designer on the product
  • Team: Designer + engineering team at Core Software Integrated
  • Scope: Research, IA, sitemap, sprint planning, end-to-end UI
  • Surface: Web admin panel + embeddable widget + companion mobile app
  • Status: Designed end-to-end, scoped into a four-phase build roadmap
The problem

Globally, the customer-engagement category was crowded, Intercom, Crisp, Drift, Zendesk, but every one of those tools shared two friction points for a Nepali business: priced in USD at seat counts most local teams couldn't justify, and built around channels, currencies, and workflows tuned for North American markets. The cheaper alternatives (Tawk.to, basic widget plugins) solved the chat box but stopped there, no shared inbox, no contact history, no marketing, no pipeline.

Local businesses ended up doing customer engagement across five disconnected apps: Facebook Messenger, WhatsApp, Viber, IG DM, and email. Conversations leaked between channels. There was no team inbox, no ticket history, no contact record tying it all together. Chatter set out to be that missing layer, a single, locally built SaaS covering support, marketing, sales, and operations end-to-end, priced for the market it served.

Anatomy of the product

Chatter is three surfaces stitched together. Each one targets a different audience, and the design work spans all three.

Embeddable widget

A JS snippet drops into any host site. End customers chat through it, anonymous or signed in, with FAQ, knowledge-base lookup, and live-agent escalation built in.

Web admin panel

The agent workspace. Shared inbox, conversation routing, contact records, marketing campaigns, sales pipeline, task boards, the operational heart of the product.

API surface

GraphQL and REST endpoints with JWE-encrypted payloads. Multi-tenant by design, one panel manages unlimited apps for unlimited sites.

A four-phase build, ordered by who needed it first

The feature set was too large to ship in one go. I worked with the team to organise it into four prioritised phases, each one mapped to a distinct user inside the customer's company. Support went first because that was the bleeding wound, everything else compounded on the foundation it laid.

1. Support team

Stop the inbox bleeding.

  • Shared team inbox
  • Messenger widget with FAQ + auto-reply
  • Knowledge base & tickets

2. Marketing team

Turn conversations into outbound.

  • Email & SMS campaigns
  • Segmentation
  • Templates & engagement analytics

3. Sales team

Convert engagement into pipeline.

  • Contact management with history
  • Tags & segments
  • Trigger-based automation

4. Management & ops

Run the team from anywhere.

  • Task boards & pipelines
  • Calendar & assignment
  • Companion mobile app

Designs by phase

Below are the designs grouped by the same four phases the build was scoped into. Each block opens with the user problem the screens were resolving, then shows the designs that answered back.

Onboarding & auth

A new SMB owner shouldn't need an IT team to start. Single-tap social sign-in, a recoverable password flow, and email verification, every step is one decision wide.

First-run: create a workspace

Chatter is multi-tenant, so the first thing a new user does is create an organisation. The empty state explains what a workspace is for; the create flow gathers the minimum needed to spin one up.

Phase 1, Team inbox

The core of the product: a shared inbox where every channel lands. Agents see the conversation list, the active thread, and the customer's right-rail profile side-by-side, with mark-as-ticket, assignment, tags, and call escalation inline. Internal team chat hangs off the same shell.

Phase 1, Channel integrations

Each external channel (Messenger, WhatsApp, Viber, web widget) has its own empty-state setup screen that walks the SMB owner through connecting their account, no engineering required.

Phase 1, Knowledge base & FAQs

Half the support volume in any SMB is repeat questions. The knowledge base lets the team write articles and tutorials, organise them by topic, and surface them inside the embeddable widget as self-serve FAQs, cutting the inbox load before a conversation even starts.

The embeddable widget itself ships in multiple variants, FAQ-first, direct-to-agent, and color-themed for different host sites, designed to feel native to whatever site it lands on.

Phase 2, Marketing & analytics

Once conversations are flowing in, they become a customer list. Marketing turns that list into outbound, engagement campaigns segmented by tag, behaviour, or conversation history. The analytics view shows performance broken down by channel: Messenger, SMS, Email.

Phase 3, Contact management

Visitors, customers, and companies all live in one filterable table with tags, segments, and primary contact channels. Clicking a row opens a full profile with personal info, conversation notes, email thread, and shared files , the audit trail a sales rep needs before picking up the phone.

The contact detail page anchors everything: personal info, notes, email thread, and files all rendered in tabs so the rep can move between context without leaving the customer.

Phase 4, Boards: pipelines & ops

Boards are where engagement becomes pipeline. Each conversation can be promoted onto a board, assigned to a teammate, deadlined, and tracked through stages. The same board surface backs both sales pipelines and operational task lists, so a single SMB owner doesn't have to context-switch between two products.

Settings & team availability

Agent availability windows, team management, integration credentials, and workspace preferences all sit in one settings surface, structured so admins can find what they need without spelunking through nested menus.

Billing, add-ons, & the marketplace

A locally priced subscription is half the pitch, the other half is optional add-ons (extra channels, automation tiers, integrations) the customer can opt into without leaving the app. The add-ons store is self-serve with a cart, so an SMB doesn't have to email sales to upgrade.

Outcome

Chatter reached a fully designed product, widget, admin panel, and the companion mobile app, scoped into a four-phase build plan that engineering could pick up sprint by sprint. The IA, design system, and screen library cover the entire feature set in the spec: support, marketing, sales, and operations.

Chatter didn't reach a public launch during my tenure at Core Software Integrated. The design was complete; the build was still in progress when I moved on. That means the work was never validated with live users, which I'm upfront about. What I can speak to is what was designed, why each decision was made, and how the roadmap was scoped to be buildable.

What I'd take into the next project
  • Define the category, don't copy one. With no incumbent to react against, the IA had to be argued from first principles. That's harder than redesigning a known product, and more formative. I'd reach for that kind of greenfield problem again.
  • Phase before you design. Scoping the build into four prioritised phases before drawing a single screen kept the design grounded in what would actually ship in which sprint, instead of polishing a feature that wasn't on the near-term roadmap.
  • Design the embed, not just the app. The widget is the only surface most end-customers ever see, it has to feel native to every host site it lands on. Designing for that variability forced earlier component thinking than a typical product would.
